text: Sure, good to see so many familiar faces and names. Panel. Yeah, it's Jan Johansson, Kellert Sessions. We've been the town's planning, engineering and wetland consultants since I believe 2008. I'm happy to do that. So if that sounds good, we can just take it step by step. So comprehensive plans, master plans, I think the terms are the same. I don't think there's any real difference between the two. So the New York State land use statutes or New York State law requires that zoning laws be adopted in accordance with the comprehensive plan. And if you wanted to get down into the weeds, you could look at town law section 272A that applies to all towns in the state of New York with relationship to definitions and processes for the adoption of comprehensive plans. The purpose of the plan or a comprehensive plan is to plan ahead, generally looking 10 years out. And the comp plan helps to remove the planning process from kind of immediate political consideration and to allow more objective analysis of community growth and needs. So you're looking at the needs of the community, looking out 10 years or so and trying to plan for that so that that plan is in place for future decisions to be made over the years by different boards, land use boards, generally planning boards, town boards, zoning board of appeals. There is a definition for what a comp plan is provided by the state. And I'll just read out this very technical definition. It is the means and materials written and or graphic, including but not limited to maps, charts, studies, resolutions, reports, and other descriptive material that identify the goals, objectives, principles, guidelines, policies, standards, devices, and instruments for the immediate and long-term, long-range protection enhancement, growth and development of the town. So generally comp plans can address or do address the goals, the objectives, and the policies of the town. They generally look at the existing and proposed land uses and their intensity. They generally, depending on the location of the community, may speak to agricultural uses, historic resources, cultural resources, natural resources, things that are worthy of protection that are important to the community. They almost always talk about the population, the demographics, and the socioeconomic trends. Transportation, utilities and infrastructure, including cell coverage, housing needs, economic development, energy, climate change. And they always, the comp plan always kind of ends in the last chapter, which is the implementation of those goals, objectives, and policies. So the meat of the document is identifying the goals and objectives, and then the last piece is how are you gonna implement that? Just, if you picked up a half a dozen comp plans in Westchester County, they would typically have, just in terms of, like if you looked at a table of contents for a typical comp plan in Westchester County, it would have a very thorough introduction, history of the town, growth patterns and projections. We have a very detailed vision statement of what the vision of the community is in the next 10 years. And there'd be a list of goals and objectives. Then there'd be separate chapters, and those chapters can kind of run the gamut, but the important items facing the community, and they could be zoning, population and housing, economics, environmental resources, community facilities, transportation, infrastructure. And within, those are typically chapters in the comprehensive plan, and within each chapter, under each category, there'd be a description of the existing condition, the projections, concerns, impacts, and recommendations associated with each category. And as I mentioned, probably the most important section following that would be the implementation section, which would identify a list of action items, really for the town board to consider over the next number of years to implement the goals and objectives of the comp plan. As important as the comp plan is, analyzing the environmental impact of the implementation of that plan. And comp plans are subject to the State Environmental Quality Review Act. They are type one actions under SEQRA, which means that it's an action that's more likely to require the preparation of an environmental impact statement, and many of them do. Generally, from what I've seen in this area anyway, in most recent years is the comp plan is prepared simultaneously with an environmental impact statement. And the environmental impact statement is evaluating, what the impact is going to be implementing that plan. And the town board in this case would have to, or is going to be required to evaluate that and come to some sort of secret determination prior to adopting the plan. And nine times out of 10, I think that communities just realize that and they simultaneously track an EIS with their comp plan. The adoption of the comp plan will require public hearing, at least one, and requires a referral to the county planning board under the general municipal law. And again, once a comp plan is adopted, all the land use regulations that come afterwards have to be consistent with that plan. And generally, the more descriptive and tighter your comprehensive plan, the more defined your land use laws will be in the future because you're providing direct direction to future land use decisions. So that's kind of just like an overall snapshot of what a comp plan is. Could take questions now.
